narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 59.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty, but it means the model judged failure more likely than passing, so the application was rejected.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. Your third-year decile of 2 is well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. The next most important factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.60, which is above the accepted-student average of about 3.23 and therefore pushed toward passing. The third factor was your LSAT score of 27, which is below the accepted-student average of about 37.2 and pushed toward failure. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on the two areas that raised concern. Consider retaking the LSAT after substantial preparation, since a stronger score would counter the strongest academic-risk signal. Seek admissions feedback and, if possible, provide context for your third-year performance or evidence of improvement. You may also strengthen your application through relevant work, academic preparation, or bar-readiness support, then reapply when your profile better demonstrates likely bar success.
